chapter_theme: Under the heading மன்னரைச் சேர்ந்தொழுகல், nineteen verses on serving kings: work owed for food already eaten and reward trusted to the commander, no contradiction and no flinching, strength borrowed from the king, not asking and not seeking elsewhere, access and timing above rank, the danger of royal love, a fallen king still a snake, no meddling between kings, no treachery, resentment kept asleep and forbearance not presumed on, and steadiness before slander.

266.reading: Addressing a woman of fine jewels, the verse asks what place there is for shrinking back from a task the bannered-chariot kings have assigned, for those who live by sharing those kings' food, since no one drinks the toddy and then goes limp.
266.nuance: கூட்டுண்டு, eating together with or from the king, makes the service a debt already taken. குழை (to soften, droop) is read here as losing nerve; the proverb may also mean that one who has drunk cannot then pretend to be sober, and the sense is not fully fixed.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who drinks toddy and then wilts

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who lives on the king's food cannot slacken on the king's work

267.reading: When the king of the victorious spear gives a command, to say 'we have received nothing' is folly; one should do the work without grievance, for it is the one who says 'do' who says 'eat'.
267.nuance: The verse answers the servant who bargains before working; reward is placed after the work and in the same mouth as the command.

pazhamozhi.literal: he who said 'do it' is the one who says 'eat'

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the servant should do the king's work first and trust the reward to follow from the one who commanded it

268.reading: When the king puts his own men at the head, saying 'let our men do this for us', they do not fall back even at the point of the spear; to answer him back is the way of saying 'pool' when he says 'aal'.
268.nuance: தமர் are the king's own people, and his putting them first is the honour that binds them. பூல் is taken as a plant name chosen for its jingle with ஆல்; the proverb mocks mere contradiction rather than reasoned dissent.

pazhamozhi.literal: when one says 'banyan', the other says 'pool'

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to contradict the king's commission is perverse contrariness in his trusted men

269.reading: Addressing the lord of the shore where palmyras with fronds stand by the full waves, the verse says that if one does not act to break away or stand off in fear, but conducts oneself so that kings hard to oppose are pleased, everything that the sea does not yield will come.
269.nuance: The address to a lord of the seashore makes the proverb pointed: even to one whose wealth comes from the sea, the king's favour yields what the sea does not. விடலமை in line 1 is read as 'acting so as to leave'; the word is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: all that is not got from the sea will be got

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: pleasing the king without flinching brings every gain

270.reading: Tasks fit to win the king's glad consent, each taken up in its proper measure, when they ripen in their fruit come back upon the one who did them, as a palm fruit when ripe falls at the foot of its parent tree.
270.nuance: The proverb has no opening quotation mark in our text; the span is taken from the closing mark and the sense. Whether செய்தான்மேல் ஏறும் means the reward or the responsibility comes to the doer is not settled by the verse; the palm image favours a return to the source.

pazhamozhi.literal: when the palm fruit ripens it falls at the foot of the tree that bore it

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the fruit of work done for the king returns to its doer

271.reading: Addressing a woman whose bright skin bears the spreading sunangu marks, the verse asks whether those who have joined mighty, proud kings will tremble in fear of any one man, for the fine horn of a strong-necked bull is sharp.
271.nuance: The horn's sharpness is put down to the neck behind it, so the servant's courage is borrowed from the king's strength rather than his own.

pazhamozhi.literal: the good horn of a bull with a strong neck is sharp

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a servant backed by a strong king need fear no single opponent

272.reading: Whoever the king esteems and is pleased with, other people too esteem in the same way; addressing a woman of soft, well-tended hair, the verse says that, as is known, the vessel into which ghee was poured is the one that pours ghee.
272.nuance: கொண்டேனை is read as கொண்டு with ஏனை மாந்தரும், 'other people too'. The verse states a fact of reputation, not a merit: esteem flows where the king has poured it.

pazhamozhi.literal: only the vessel that has been filled with ghee pours ghee

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: honour conferred by the king is passed on by others to the one he favoured

273.reading: Those who have joined manly kings should not, even when they fall into hardship, say 'we want something here'; addressing a man whose chest bears ornaments, the verse says that for the worthy, not wanting gives all that is wanted.
273.nuance: வேண்டாமை is the word of the renouncer's ethics, here put to use at court: the paradox is that freedom from wanting is the surest way to be given. அல்லுறினும் is read as 'even if they suffer distress'.

pazhamozhi.literal: not wanting brings all that one wants

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the worthy servant who asks nothing of the king even in want receives everything

274.reading: For those who have served the guardian king fully and stay doing the work he commands, to seek help from elsewhere is like a calf standing by its cow and sucking her throat while the udder is there.
274.nuance: உதவு அடுத்தல் is read as approaching others for help; the line could also mean that others' help to such servants is superfluous. Either way the king is the udder.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like sucking the mother's throat while the udder is there

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the king's servant who seeks support elsewhere turns from the true source to a dry one

275.reading: There is nothing that cannot be achieved by those who watch the right moment with distinguished kings and speak with skill; even those who are like life itself to victorious kings fare worse outside, for a hunchback inside is better than a minister outside.
275.nuance: The kūn, a hunchbacked palace attendant, has the inner rooms and so the king's moments; the minister, however high, does not. The verse ranks nearness at the right time above office. Line 2 உரைப்பாரைக்கொன் (று) is read as உரைப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று.

pazhamozhi.literal: a hunchback within is better than a minister without

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: access and timing in speaking to the king outweigh rank and even dearness

276.reading: To think 'the kings of the parasol chariots will suit us', and, when they love one fiercely, to return the love and strive on without perceiving anything that lies hidden, is like clearing one's throat at a dangerous moment.
276.nuance: The proverb is short and its image cannot be fixed: கடிய may be 'dangerous' or 'quickly', and கனைத்தல் a cough or a neigh. The counsel is clearer than the proof: royal love is not a ground for unguarded action.

pazhamozhi.literal: giving a cough where it is dangerous to make a sound

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the favourite who trusts the king's love and does not read what it hides betrays himself

277.reading: Even if a worthy king has lost all his greatness, those who weigh his station do not face him and mock him, even when he has gone without his great kin and stands alone, for no one slights a snake because it is small.
277.nuance: நிலைநோக்கி, 'looking to his standing', makes the restraint a judgement of what he still is and may again be; இளைது can mean small or young, and the snake keeps its venom either way.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one belittles a snake for being young

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a fallen and friendless king keeps his power to strike and must not be scorned

278.reading: To enter among proud kings and speak words that help neither of them is something one cannot afterwards set right for oneself, and that is the bringing of harm: it is eating straw between bulls.
278.nuance: ஒருத்தற்கு உதவாத சொல் is read as words of no use to either party; it may instead mean words that fail the one king one serves. தீதரம் is unusual and is read as a form of தீது, harm.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who meddles between rival kings is crushed between them

279.reading: For those who served many days and secretly took and ate what was the king's to come before him with gold tied up as an offering, hoping he will do them no harm, is tying a water lily with its own fibre.
279.nuance: The image works because the lily is bound by what grew from it: the gift that is meant to win the king over was the king's own. The verse does not say whether the trick succeeds, only what it is.

pazhamozhi.literal: tying the blue water lily with its own stalk-fibre

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to placate the king with gold taken from him is to give him back what was his

280.reading: Those who were highly regarded for standing in truth, if they go on doing dark deeds under the king's very hand and take up falsehood, setting themselves against him, fell the palm so that it falls on themselves.
280.nuance: The servant's standing was built on truth (மெய்ம்மையே நின்று), so his falsehood fells the very trunk that held him up. Our text has a full stop inside the closing quotation mark.

pazhamozhi.literal: they cut down the palm so that it falls on them

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the trusted servant who turns false brings his own ruin

281.reading: Even if the fiercely angry king does what one does not want, one should not act in the least on what one holds in the heart, even when one has been caught for whatever one did, for no one wakes a sleeping tiger from its sleep.
281.nuance: The resentment is granted as real (வேண்டாதவே செயினும்); the counsel is to keep it inside, since the king's quiet anger is the sleeping tiger. Line 3 என்செய்து அகப்பட்டக் கண்ணும் is read as 'whatever one is caught for'.

pazhamozhi.literal: would anyone rouse a sleeping tiger from its sleep

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a servant wronged by the king should not stir the king's anger by acting on his grievance

282.reading: Why should those who cannot even protect themselves by themselves be angry with kings of leaping horses? Addressing the lord of a beautiful hill where wild cattle leap, the verse says that those who have climbed the kongu tree have no safety.
282.nuance: Why the kongu gives no safety (brittle wood or thorny trunk) the verse does not say. வாமான்றோ is read as வாம் மான் தேர், the king of leaping horses and chariots.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who have climbed the kongu tree find no safety

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the weak who turn against the king have no refuge

283.reading: When the king, though seeming unable to bear it, bears with those who have done what does not suit him, to go on doing more and more of what cannot be borne is a boil risen upon a hump.
283.nuance: The verse turns on பொறாஅன் போலப் பொறுத்தல்: the king's patience is shown with displeasure, and the servant who reads only the patience compounds the fault.

pazhamozhi.literal: a boil that has risen on a hump

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: to presume on the king's forbearance heaps a second affliction on the first

284.reading: Beyond working out how the king may see clearly through the false slander spoken by worthless men, the wise do not dance along with those who rise up in alarm and dance, like the stilts of a dancer to the drum.
284.nuance: பொய்க்கால் is read as the stilts of a stilt-dancer, which move only as the dancer moves them; the proverb mocks those who are carried by another's alarm. The pun on பொய் (false) links the stilts to the false slander.

pazhamozhi.literal: like the false legs of a dancer to the drum

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the king's servant as a type

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the wise courtier does not move with the agitation that slander raises but helps the king discern

links.note: Purananuru 290 has a warrior's king give him toddy before drinking himself, and the warrior will take the spear meant for the king; Pazhamozhi 266 turns the toddy already drunk into the reason a king's man cannot shrink from his task.
links.teaches: Held together they show the heroic custom of the king's toddy hardening into a courtier's proverb of obligation: what the war poem offers as honour freely returned, the ethics verse states as a debt that forbids hesitation.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 266 says those who have eaten the king's food cannot shirk his work; 267 says those who have not yet been rewarded cannot refuse it either, since the one who commands will feed.
links.teaches: Read together the two verses close both exits from service: the servant who has been paid owes the work, and the servant who has not been paid owes it too, so reward never becomes a condition the servant may set.

links.note: Naladiyar 167 says those who keep close to kings enjoy their wealth without needing to be worthy; Pazhamozhi 272 says whomever the king esteems the people esteem as well.
links.teaches: The pair shows royal nearness conferring not only goods but public standing: the Naladiyar's unworthy favourite gets the king's wealth, and Pazhamozhi adds that he gets the town's regard too, poured on from the king like ghee from a filled pot.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the ghee-filled vessel makes honour a thing that passes from container to container, adding the public as a second recipient that the quatrain's image of shade-giving trees does not have.

links.note: Kural 363 says there is no fine wealth like not wanting, here or hereafter; Pazhamozhi 273 uses the same word வேண்டாமை to say that a king's servant who asks nothing even in hardship is given all he wants.
links.teaches: Together they show the renouncer's highest wealth being turned into a courtier's method: the Kural's not-wanting is its own reward, while Pazhamozhi makes it the means by which a king's servant is given everything, so the same virtue serves release and preferment.
links.list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the chapter on cutting off desire into service at court and adds the case of hardship (அல்லுறினும்), where not asking is hardest.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 273 says the king's servant should ask the king for nothing; 274 says he should not seek help elsewhere either, for that is like sucking the cow's throat while the udder is there.
links.teaches: Taken together the verses leave the servant no one to ask: not the king, whom he must not petition, and not others, who are a dry source, so all his provision must come unasked from the master he serves.

links.note: Kural 696 asks the king's counsellor to know the mood and the time before saying what is needed; Pazhamozhi 275 says those who speak to kings at the right moment achieve everything, and that a hunchback inside is better than a minister outside.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the couplet's timing depends on access: one who knows the right moment is useless unless he is in the room when it comes, so the menial with the inner rooms can outdo the minister the Kural addresses.
links.list_adds: its proverb ranks a hunchbacked attendant above a minister, adding a ranking by nearness that cuts across office, which the couplet's advice on timing does not consider.

links.note: Kural 691 asks those who serve kings to be like people warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Pazhamozhi 276 warns the favourite who answers the king's fierce love with his own and acts without perceiving what lies hidden.
links.teaches: Together they show that the danger of being too near comes most from the king's own affection: the Kural's fire burns those who press close, and Pazhamozhi shows the courtier being drawn close by love and forgetting to keep distance.
links.list_adds: it gives the too-near case a cause the couplet leaves out, the king's love itself, and closes it with a proverb of self-betrayal.

links.note: Kural 698 forbids belittling a king as young or as close kin; Pazhamozhi 277 forbids mocking a king who has lost his greatness and his kin and stands alone, for no one slights a snake as small.
links.teaches: The pair extends the Kural's bar on belittling from youth and kinship to ruin and isolation, and the proverb's இளைது echoes the couplet's இளையர: in both, smallness of age or fortune is no licence, but Pazhamozhi grounds this in the power still in him, the Kural in the light of his station.
links.list_adds: it moves the couplet's case from a young king in his strength to a fallen king without kin, and gives a reason by fear of the snake where the couplet gives one by the dignity of the office.

links.note: Naladiyar 241 says the worthy feel shame and do not advance on humbled enemies, as the eclipse snake does not seize the crescent moon; Pazhamozhi 277 says those who serve a fallen king do not mock him, as no one slights a young snake.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two snakes give two different grounds for sparing the fallen: in the Naladiyar the strong one is the snake and holds back from shame, in Pazhamozhi the fallen king is the snake and is spared from fear, so restraint before the weak may be nobility or prudence.
links.list_adds: it turns the quatrain's image around, making the humbled one the snake, so the same restraint is grounded in the danger of the weak rather than the shame of the strong.

links.note: Kural 700 says the intimacy that does improper things on the ground of old acquaintance brings ruin; Pazhamozhi 280 says those trusted for their truth who turn to falsehood against the king fell the palm onto themselves.
links.teaches: The pair names two kinds of capital a servant can spend against himself: the Kural's long familiarity and Pazhamozhi's reputation for truth, and in both the very ground of trust becomes the instrument of the fall.
links.list_adds: its palm that falls on the one who fells it makes the ruin self-inflicted by the servant's own act, where the couplet says only that the intimacy brings ruin.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 270 has the ripe palm fruit fall at the foot of its parent tree, and 280 has the felled palm fall on the feller; both use a falling palm for a deed returning to its doer.
links.teaches: Together the two palm images show one law of return working both ways in the king's service: work done in measure comes back like ripe fruit to its tree, and treachery comes back like a felled trunk on the axeman.

links.note: Purananuru 73 has Nalankilli say the fool who scorned him will hardly escape, like a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; Pazhamozhi 281 tells the king's wronged servant not to wake the sleeping tiger by acting on his grievance.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the same sleeping tiger from both sides: the Chola king boasts of being the tiger that the careless rouse to their death, and the ethics verse teaches the king's own servant to treat that tiger as a standing danger to be left asleep.

links.note: Naladiyar 164 says those who have angered the great do not escape even in a strong fortress, as the snake in its crevice dreads the thunder; Pazhamozhi 282 asks why those who cannot protect themselves are angry with kings at all.
links.teaches: The pair runs the danger the other way: the Naladiyar speaks of those who have provoked the great and find no shelter, Pazhamozhi of those who themselves feel anger at the king, and both conclude that against royal power the weak have no refuge.
links.list_adds: it shifts the quatrain's case from another's wrath to one's own anger, and its kongu tree makes the refuge something the angry man climbs himself.

links.note: Kural 699 says the clear-sighted do not do the unacceptable on the thought that they are in favour; Pazhamozhi 283 says that when a king bears an offence with visible displeasure, going on to offend again is a boil on a hump.
links.teaches: Together they mark two false grounds for presuming: favour in the Kural and forgiveness in Pazhamozhi; the ethics verse adds that the king's patience, shown with displeasure, is a warning the offender misreads as licence.
links.list_adds: it adds a sequence the couplet lacks, a first offence borne and then repeated, and a proverb of harm piled on harm.

links.note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a flame in a lamp; Pazhamozhi 284 says the wise do not join those agitated by slander spoken to the king, but work out how he may see through it.
links.teaches: The pair moves steadiness under slander from one's own mind to the court: the Naladiyar's pure heart is not moved when slandered, and Pazhamozhi's wise courtier is not moved when another is slandered before the king, and also helps the king see clearly.
links.list_adds: it gives the steady one a task beyond composure, clearing the king's judgement, and sets him against a crowd of stilt-dancers moved by alarm.

source_issues: 270 lines 3-4: the proverb has a closing quotation mark but no opening one; the span பனைமுதிரின் ... விடும் is inferred.
275 line 2: உரைப்பாரைக்கொன் (று) looks like a misprint for உரைப்பார்க்கொன்று.
280 line 4: a full stop stands inside the closing quotation mark.
269 line 1: விடலமை is doubtful; 276 line 4: the proverb கடிய கனைத்து விடல் is obscure; 278 line 3: தீதரம் is unusual.
273 line 1: மன்னரைத் சார்ந்தார் has தச் where sandhi expects ச் (மன்னரைச் சார்ந்தார்).
